work_order.understanding:
QA failed PR #59 on five bugs (BUG-5 to BUG-9) and on the AC-11 spelling sweep T-14, which compared 82 selectors against Chromium in both directions. I reproduced every one of them myself on d923294: the clean tree is 81 pass / 0 fail, and I ran twelve selector mutations one at a time. I then measured each disputed case in a real Chromium against the served page instead of taking the report's numbers, and that mattered twice.

WAS THE v2 DIAGNOSIS WRONG? Partly, and in a way that accounts for all five. v2's diagnosis - the guard decides "is this the page h1" from the spelling of a selector rather than from the element, and never compares the value the browser settles on - was correct, and it fixed BUG-1 to BUG-4. Those four stay fixed: T-3 to T-13 all pass on this run. But v2 put the safety property in the wrong place. Its contract was "reachability is false only on a proof", and it applied that to the MATCHER. A matcher can only return a sound proof if what fed it is faithful and complete, and v2 left both of those unfixed by design:

1. The reader was knowingly left partial. v2's own out_of_scope says it: "At-rules other than @media and @supports. @layer, @container and @scope are walked as opaque blocks, exactly as in attempt 1, and none appears in the shipped stylesheet." BUG-5 is that deferred gap arriving on schedule. v2's understanding claimed in the same breath that the rewrite "has a shape that cannot fail this way" - true of the matcher, false of the pipeline, because a rule the reader never hands the matcher can be neither proved nor reported at all.

2. The tokenizer does not decode CSS. splitSimple matches an id or class with /^[A-Za-z_-][\w-]*/, which stops at a backslash, so '#\6d ain' is read as the literal text '#\6d ain'. The danger is not that it misreads; it is that a decode failure does not become "undecided". The backslash is consumed as an unknown token and the surviving fragment 'ain' is then read as a TYPE selector that no ancestor satisfies - a confident false. That is a proof fabricated out of a decode failure, which is the one thing the contract forbids. BUG-8.

3. Two of the guard's own entry points opt out of the rule they were written under. stripNarrowing deletes a pseudo-class AND ITS ARGUMENT, so ':where(h1)' reduces to the empty compound, and "an empty compound matches anything" is the hazard v2's own comment names above that function for ':root' and leaves open. And isClassBranch returns true for any single compound carrying the class token without ever calling branchReaches, so '.page-title::after' and '.page-title[data-x]' are admitted as the class rule itself. BUG-6 and BUG-7.

So the diagnosis is rewritten. v2 did not build a wrong guard; it built half of one. The one-directional property was asserted on the matcher and never stated over the reader and the tokenizer, and two predicates bypassed the reach test they were governed by. BUG-5 and BUG-8 are false passes; BUG-6 and BUG-7 are false alarms; both directions are the same missing statement. This is a different fix from patching the five sites, and approach sets out why.

THIS IS NOT THE "CRITERION IS WRONG" CASE, and I want that on the record before the criteria below. AC-11's how_to_verify already names '.page-title::after' in its PROVABLY NO-MATCH list, and already requires "a probe over every rule in src/web/styles.css declaring font-size, line-height, margin or font names '.page-title' and nothing else as reaching the h1". The criteria were right and the code contradicted them. AC-1 to AC-12 are carried forward byte-for-byte, none renumbered and none dropped. On a third pass the temptation is to move the goalposts, and here that would be wrong: a criterion edited to match a false alarm is the artefact this pipeline can least afford, because every future QA run would then certify the defect.

WHAT I MEASURED, AND THE TWO PLACES IT CAME OUT DIFFERENTLY FROM THE REPORT.

1. 'h1[data\2d testid="page-title"]' moves the h1 to 38.4px in the browser and the suite is RED on it - but for the wrong reason, the value cross-check rather than reachability, exactly as QA suspected. After this change it must stay red, and now for the right reason.

2. '#mai\6e h1 { font-size: 2.4rem; }' - I expected this to be a sixth false pass, because it decodes to '#main h1' and every instinct says it should move the title. It does not. The browser reads 22.4px, and QA's matrix records it as not moving. A hex escape CONSUMES the whitespace that terminates it, so '#mai\6e h1' is the single id '#mainh1', which matches nothing; '#\6d ain h1' is the id '#main' followed by the type 'h1', and does move the title to 38.4px. That pair is all of BUG-8 in one line, and it is the test that distinguishes a tokenizer that DECODES CSS from one that merely stopped crashing: a fix that splits on that space gets the first case right for the wrong reason and the second one wrong. Both are pinned in AC-17.

3. Descending into every at-rule is NOT the fix, and it would add three false alarms. I measured each: '@container c { h1 { font-size: 2.4rem !important } }' leaves the h1 at 22.4px (no container exists), '@starting-style { h1 { font-size: 2.4rem !important } }' leaves it at 22.4px (a starting style is beaten by any normal declaration, important or not), and a prelude-less '@scope { ... }' leaves it at 22.4px. Only @layer moves the title, and only when the declaration is !important. So the at-rule work is a small rule table with a reason attached to each entry, not "read everything" - and each entry is pinned on both sides in AC-13 and AC-14.

4. Layering also changes which CLASS-rule declaration wins, which nothing in the guard models. '@layer base { .page-title { font-size: 2.4rem; } }' leaves the h1 at 22.4px, because the unlayered shipped rule outranks a layered NORMAL declaration whatever its specificity - '@layer base { #main h1 { font-size: 2.4rem; } }' is clean for the same reason, (1,0,1) losing to (0,1,0). The reverse holds for !important: '@layer base { h1 { font-size: 2.4rem !important; } }' reaches 38.4px, because importance reverses the layer order, and a layered important beats an unlayered important as well. A fix that reads @layer blocks but leaves layer rank out of the cascade would make the first of those a false alarm and the second a false pass, in one change. This is the part of BUG-5 that is not a one-line 'read the block' fix.

5. A same-value restatement at higher specificity is reported today and changes nothing. 'h1[data-testid] { font-size: 1.4rem }', '#main h1 { font-size: 1.4rem }', '#main h1 { line-height: 1.25 }' and '#main h1 { margin: 0 }' all read 22.4px / 28px / 0px, and the guard's message for them - "the page h1's font-size would be font-size: 1.4rem instead of font-size: 1.4rem" - is self-refuting. This is BUG-3 from v1, one level up: the report is about a SELECTOR when it should be about a VALUE. The exception that must not be relaxed is a shorthand - '#main h1 { font: 700 1.4rem system-ui; }' keeps the font-size at 22.4px but drops the line-height to normal (24px), and '#main h1 { all: unset; }' takes the h1 to 16px/24px/0px - so a shorthand restatement is never a restatement, and a rule that silenced it would trade a false alarm for a false pass.

6. ':root { all: revert; }' is reported and moves nothing (root 16px, h1 22.4px). revert REMOVES author declarations rather than setting one, so it can only move the root back toward the user-agent default the class rule's rem is measured against.

7. '@media print { #main h1 { font-size: 2.4rem; } }' is reported and does not move the served page. I could have left this alone - v2 kept @media lifting deliberately - but then the sweep flags it on the next run too. The guard models the page as served in a browser on screen, which is the environment AC-1 is verified in and the one the whole contract is written about; print and speech are definitionally not that medium. A feature condition is a different thing: '(max-width: 900px)' and '(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)' are undecidable here, so they stay on the reported side with the condition named, which is the direction a false alarm is allowed to fall in. The cost is real - a print-only override of the page title is no longer reported by the suite - so it is written into AC-14 and into risks rather than left for the next person to discover.

Nothing here is a defect in the shipped app. src/web/pages.js:57 and src/web/styles.css:137 are correct as shipped, this change touches neither, and the browser reads 22.4px / 28px / 0px on the clean tree across all 25 shells.
work_order.root_cause:
The guard this file carries is three layers - a READER that flattens the stylesheet into rules, a TOKENIZER that splits a selector into simple selectors, and a MATCHER that asks whether one of them can match the page h1. v2 rebuilt the matcher and left the other two as they were, then wrote its safety contract as "reachability is false only on a proof" - a property of the matcher alone. The property is a property of the pipeline. A proof is only a proof if it is a fact about the element that a faithful decode of the sheet established, and there is no proof at all to return about a rule the reader never produced. All five new bugs are one of three ways that statement was never made.

BUG-5 and BUG-8 are the reader and the tokenizer. readStylesheet's walker recurses on /^@(media|supports)\b/ and otherwise drops any prelude beginning with '@', so an @layer block is consumed whole by the brace matcher and never descended into - as are @container, @scope and @starting-style. The guard is therefore reasoning about a strict subset of the sheet, and everything outside that subset is unreportable by construction. A second and less obvious hole sits in the same layer: layer RANK is not part of the cascade the guard computes. beats() and keptInPool() order declarations by importance, then specificity, then document position, and none of those three encodes that an unlayered NORMAL declaration outranks a layered one whatever its specificity while a layered !IMPORTANT is outranked by nothing in the sheet. So even a correct 'read the block' fix reports '@layer base { .page-title { font-size: 2.4rem } }' (the browser reads 22.4px - the unlayered shipped rule wins) and stays silent on '@layer base { h1 { font-size: 2.4rem !important } }' (38.4px). That is a false alarm and a false pass produced by the same omission. The tokenizer's half is splitSimple: it recognises id, class, attribute, type, universal, pseudo and pseudo-element by regex over the raw text, and it has no notion of a CSS escape at all. A backslash is not a character it can read, so it is consumed as an unknown token and the fragment after it is re-read as something else - 'ain' as a type selector in '#\6d ain h1'. Because a type selector that no ancestor satisfies is a confident false, a DECODE FAILURE IS CONVERTED INTO A PROOF. That is the precise inversion of the contract, and it is why the whole approach is to decode rather than to widen.

BUG-6 and BUG-7 are the two predicates that bypass the rule. isClassBranch answers 'is this the class rule' from the rightmost compound's token list alone: if that compound carries a '.page-title' token and the branch is a single compound, it is admitted, with no reachability question asked. So '.page-title::after' - which the browser proves does not style the element at all, since a pseudo-element styles a generated box - and '.page-title[data-x]', which the h1 does not satisfy, are both taken to BE the class rule. Their declarations are pooled as the baseline and cross-checked against the held value, and the value cross-check then reports an override of a rule the shipped stylesheet does not have. The companion symptom is the same predicate reached from the other side: ground (a) skips a branch that isClassBranch claims, so a real competitor sharing a rule with the class branch is invisible. stripNarrowing is the second bypass. It removes every pseudo-class token except ':root' to reach 'the base', but it removes the ARGUMENT with it, so ':where(h1)' becomes the empty string, and compoundMatches on the empty string is a vacuous true - 'an empty compound matches anything', which is the hazard named in the comment directly above the function and left open. Every functional pseudo-class carries the same defect (':root:not(html)', 'h1:not([data-testid])'), and each produces a report whose message asserts as fact a change the browser does not make.

The last cause is not a bypass but a missing question, and it is what the spelling sweep found beyond the filed bugs. The guard's report decision is made from the SELECTOR - may it reach the h1, does it outrank the class rule - and never from the resulting VALUE, except for the class rule's own winning declaration. So 'h1[data-testid] { font-size: 1.4rem }' is reported at (0,1,1) over (0,1,0) with the message "the page h1's font-size would be font-size: 1.4rem instead of font-size: 1.4rem". The same missing comparison applies on the root side, where 'all' is treated as a set whether or not its argument is one: ':root { all: revert }' is reported and cannot change anything, because revert removes author declarations rather than declaring one. This is BUG-3 from v1 restated one level up, and v2 fixed the instance at the class rule without stating the rule.

Underneath all of it is one thing the file never says out loud: the guard's subject is one page rendered by one browser, and every claim it makes is a claim about the value that page ends up with. Each of the five bugs is a place where a value the guard asserts is not the value the page has - four in one direction, one in the other. The contract that prevents them is not "be careful with selectors". It is: the reader must produce every rule in the sheet, the tokenizer must decode the sheet's escapes rather than guess at them, every predicate that answers a question about an element must go through the same reachability function or prove why it need not, and a report must be about a value.
work_order.approach:
Test-only, confined to test/web/pages.test.js. The production files are correct and are not touched: src/web/pages.js:57 and src/web/styles.css:137 hold on every 25 shells, and the browser reads 22.4px / 28px / 0px on the clean tree.

This is not v2's approach with the five sites tightened, and the difference is structural rather than a matter of care. v2 rebuilt the MATCHER and kept the reader, the tokenizer and the value comparison, then put the safety property on the matcher alone. This rebuilds all four layers under one stated contract, so the property is a property of the pipeline:

  THE GUARD'S CONTRACT, in one place, because AC-11, the tests and the failure messages must not disagree about it. The guard reads src/web/styles.css, resolves the page h1 from the rendered markup, and reports a rule when and only when that rule would change the value the page h1 ends up with - a value in font-size, line-height or a top margin, or the value of the root's font-size that the rems are measured against. Every step between the sheet and that verdict is one-directional: a step may SKIP a rule only on a proof, a step may REPORT a rule it cannot decide about, and a step may never manufacture a proof it did not decode. The two halves are the same rule read in opposite directions, and both are pinned on both sides in the tests.

1 - A total reader, with a rule table instead of a two-name regex. readStylesheet keeps its flat document-order output and its atRules list for the message, and gains a per-at-rule decision with a stated reason for each. Nested blocks are walked to any depth, so a rule inside '@layer base { @media (max-width: 900px) { ... } }' is read. The table:
  - @media - descend. The MEDIUM is decided: a condition naming 'print' or 'speech' is a proof of non-match, because the guard's subject is a page rendered on screen, and the message is not needed. Any other condition ('all', 'screen', a feature query, an empty condition) is undecidable, so the rule is read and the condition is named in the message, which is the existing behaviour for max-width and reduced-motion and must not change.
  - @supports - descend, undecidable, condition named. Unchanged.
  - @layer - descend, and carry the layer on every rule it produces (section 2). This is the false pass.
  - @starting-style - descend, but rank the rules BELOW every normal author declaration. A starting style is beaten by any normal declaration for the same property, important or not, so it can never outrank the class rule; the rules are read rather than skipped, and the rank makes them lose. Verified with !important on the starting style: the h1 still reads 22.4px.
  - @container - descend, but silent unless the sheet declares a container anywhere ('container', 'container-type' or 'container-name' in any declaration body). With no container in the sheet a container query has nothing to match, which is a proof; with one, the rules are read and the query is named. This is a two-line check and it is what keeps the fix from adding a false alarm.
  - @scope - descend, and decide the PRELUDE with the existing reachability function against the same chain: a prelude the chain provably fails ('.nope') is a proof of non-match and the block is silent; any other prelude, including an absent one, is undecidable and the rules are read with the scope named. Note the measured asymmetry, which is a property of the engine rather than of the guard: '@scope (main) { h1 { ... } }' moves the h1 to 38.4px because the h1 is inside main, while a prelude-less '@scope' does not apply here. The guard reports the second as undecidable, which is the noisy direction and the correct one.
  - @keyframes, @font-face, @page, @property, @counter-style, @charset, @import - skip the body with a comment saying why: they describe an animation, a font, a page box or a registration, not a rendered element, so nothing inside them is a declaration on the page h1. @keyframes already is; the rest join it.
  Every entry in this table is pinned on BOTH sides in tests, because a table read only on the reporting side is how the last three bugs happened.

2 - Layer rank joins the cascade, not just the reader. beats() and keptInPool() currently order by importance, then specificity, then document position. Layer rank goes in as the FIRST comparison within an origin, and it inverts with importance, which is the whole subtlety:
  - among NORMAL declarations, unlayered beats every layer, whatever the specificity; among layers, the later-declared layer wins.
  - among !IMPORTANT declarations, layered beats unlayered; among layers, the later-declared layer wins.
  - the anonymous layer (a '@layer { }' block with no name) is ordered after every named layer declared before it.
  Measured, and both directions are wrong without this: '@layer base { #main h1 { font-size: 2.4rem; } }' is CLEAN (the (1,0,1) loses to the unlayered (0,1,0) class rule) and '@layer base { h1 { font-size: 2.4rem !important; } }' is RED at 38.4px. Because the class rule's own winner is chosen by the same function, this also fixes the value cross-check: '@layer base { .page-title { font-size: 2.4rem; } }' currently reports 2.4rem and must stop, because the unlayered shipped rule is the one the cascade keeps. Declare the layer list once, in document order, as the reader meets it, and have both the competitor comparison and the class-rule winner selection read it.

3 - A scanner that DECODES, in place of the regex vocabulary in splitSimple. Keep splitSimple's token shape and its three-way answer, and change only how a name is read. Two rules, both pinned:
  - an escape is consumed as part of the name it appears in. A backslash begins either a hex escape (one to six hex digits, plus one following whitespace which is CONSUMED) or a backslash followed by any single character, which stands for that character. '#\6d ain' is the id 'main' and the space that follows the escape is the escape's terminator, not a compound boundary. '#mai\6e h1' is the single id 'mainh1' - the escape ate the space, so there is nothing to split on - and matches nothing. That asymmetry is the bug and the test; a scanner that keeps splitting on that space gets one of the two right for the wrong reason.
  - a name that still cannot be decoded is an 'unknown' token, and simpleMatches already returns null for one, which compoundMatches already carries upward as undecided. What changes is that no undecoded fragment may be RE-READ as a type selector: the scanner consumes an escape as one unit, so 'ain' in '#\6d ain' is never offered to the type branch. Add the assertion that an 'unknown' token can never yield false, so this cannot be undone silently.
  The escape is consumed in the compound splitter as well as the tokenizer - they share one scanner, as section 4 of v2 established and this keeps - so the whitespace terminator is not a boundary anywhere.

4 - One reachability function, and no predicate beside it. branchReaches keeps its signature and its one-directional guarantee. The two predicates that bypassed it are brought under it:
  - isClassBranch must ask the same question. A branch is the class rule only if the class token is on the rightmost compound AND that branch reaches the h1 - which for a single compound means the rest of the compound must hold for the h1. '.page-title::after' is out because a pseudo-element styles a generated box; '.page-title[data-x]' is out because the h1 carries no data-x. The 'parts.length === 1' shortcut is deleted, not amended. The reach check must also be the one that is asked for a multi-compound branch, so a class rule written 'h1.page-title' or 'main > .page-title' is still found - that is what the coordinated rename and AC-3 depend on, and it is the case to re-run first.
  - stripNarrowing stops destroying information. A pseudo-class is no longer removed with its argument; it is DECIDED, and the answer depends on the pseudo-class:
    * ':not(sel)' - the element must match sel for the compound to be false, so evaluate sel as a selector list and negate. 'h1:not([data-testid])' is a proof of non-match on this h1; ':root:not(html)' is a proof against the root.
    * ':is(sel)' and ':where(sel)' - evaluate the argument as a selector list, un-negated. ':where(h1)' against the document root is then a proof of non-match, which is the fix for BUG-7, and against the h1 it is a match at (0,0,0) that loses the cascade. ':where()' contributes NO specificity; ':is()' and ':not()' contribute the specificity of their most specific argument, which compoundSpecificity must already be doing (the comment above heavier says it is, and a12 and a13 depend on it - verify rather than assume).
    * ':has(sel)' - needs descendants the chain does not carry, so it is undecidable: may match, reported. That is a false alarm on this page, which measures 22.4px for 'h1:has(> span)', and it is the direction the contract permits.
    * a plain pseudo-class (':hover', ':focus', ':nth-child(2)', anything undecidable from static markup) - decide on the base compound and return may-match, as today.
    The invariant that replaces the old comment: a compound is NEVER reduced to the empty string by this function. If the code ever produces one, it must return undecidable rather than vacuous true. That single assertion is what closes BUG-7 for good, and it should be a test.

5 - The report becomes a statement about a VALUE. Both grounds keep what they already are - (a) may match the h1 and outranks the class rule, (b) may match the root and declares font-size or font - and both gain one filter at the point where the offender is pushed: the declaration that wins for that group must carry the value the group is held at. Implement it by widening PAGE_TITLE_HELD from 'property: value' to a list of equivalent texts per group, and comparing the winning declaration's text against it with !important stripped, exactly as the class-rule cross-check already does:
  - font-size: 'font-size: 1.4rem'
  - line-height: 'line-height: 1.25'
  - margin-top: 'margin: 0', 'margin-top: 0', 'margin-block-start: 0'
  A restatement is silent, so 'h1[data-testid] { font-size: 1.4rem }' and '#main h1 { margin-top: 0 }' stop being reported and their self-refuting messages stop existing. Three cases must NOT be caught by this and are asserted alongside: a declaration on a SHORTHAND is always reported, because the shorthand sets more than the group it is filed under - '#main h1 { font: 700 1.4rem system-ui; }' leaves the h1's font-size at 22.4px and drops its line-height to normal, and '#main h1 { all: unset; }' takes it to 16px; and an 'all' whose value is exactly 'revert' is not a set at all, so ':root { all: revert; }' is silent, because revert removes author declarations rather than declaring one and so can only move the root back toward the user-agent default the class rule's rem is measured against. 'revert-layer' and 'unset' are NOT in that exemption and stay reported.

6 - Pin the whole thing, both directions, and pin the pinner. Every case above is a test, each with its browser number in the comment beside it: the twelve mutations I ran, the @layer pair from section 2 in both directions, the '#\6d ain' / '#mai\6e' pair from section 3, the four at-rules from section 1 in both directions, the functional pseudo-classes from section 4 including the two that must stay reported, the restatement set and the two shorthands that must not be silenced, and the empty-compound invariant. Keep all ~25 existing guard cases and re-run the four QA-fixed ones (T-3 to T-6) unchanged - they are the regression suite for v2's work and this change must not disturb them. Add the second anchor to the pinning test at test/web/pages.test.js:1608 so the 25-shell 'exactly one h1' assertion cannot be deleted with the suite green (BUG-9): the test currently anchors on one literal and protects one line, so a second anchor for the count assertion is the whole fix. Write the anchor unsplittable, the way the existing one is, so a deletion fails on the assertion that names what went missing rather than on a secondary one.

7 - Keep what was already right. The element chain resolved from the rendered markup, the quote- and bracket-aware splitter, the !important asymmetry within an origin, the winner-selection rule across several class rules, the @media and @supports condition naming, the shorthand-to-group reporting, the message wording that names the selector and the property, the three pinning tests for the class extractor, the call site and the class-name exception, and the class-to-rule link that keeps a coordinated rename green. Do not re-derive them; re-run them.

The class rule's own winner goes through the same comparison, so a layered .page-title no longer wins over the unlayered shipped one. The green case is the one that looks like it should be red and is not, and it is the test that says whether the fix decodes CSS or merely stopped crashing: a hex escape CONSUMES the whitespace that terminates it, so '#mai\6e h1' is the single id '#mainh1' and matches nothing, while '#\6d ain h1' is the id '#main' followed by the type 'h1'. A tokenizer that splits on that space gets this case right for the wrong reason and the first one wrong. Also confirm 'h1[data-x="a b"]' (AC-10) still reads as one compound and stays green, that nothing throws 'the cascade guard cannot read the selector', and that a token the guard cannot decode is never turned into a proof of non-match. Revert.

acceptance.check: The guard reports a rule that would change the value the page title is held at, not one that merely outranks it. Appending 'h1[data-testid] { font-size: 1.4rem; }', '#main h1 { font-size: 1.4rem; }', '#main h1 { line-height: 1.25; }', '#main h1 { margin: 0; }', '#main h1 { margin-top: 0; }', '#main h1 { margin-block-start: 0; }' and ':root { all: revert; }' each leave the suite green, and the same selectors declaring 2.4rem, 1.6 or 24px still fail
acceptance.how_to_verify: Append one at a time and run node --test; 0 failures for the seven green cases, each of which the browser renders at fontSize 22.4px / lineHeight 28px / marginTop 0px. Each of the first six restates the value the class rule already holds, so a report would carry a self-refuting message ('would be font-size: 1.4rem instead of font-size: 1.4rem'); margin-top and margin-block-start count as restatements of 'margin: 0' for the margin-top group. ':root { all: revert }' is green for a different reason: revert REMOVES author declarations rather than setting one, so it cannot move the root away from the user-agent default the class rule's rem is measured against (root reads 16px, h1 22.4px). The exception that must NOT be relaxed is a shorthand: appending '#main h1 { font: 700 1.4rem system-ui; }' must still fail, because the font shorthand leaves the h1's font-size at 22.4px but drops its line-height to 'normal' (24px), and '#main h1 { all: unset; }' must still fail, taking the h1 to 16px/24px/0px. A restatement rule that also silenced shorthands would be a false pass. Revert.

risks: The escape decoder is the load-bearing new code and the pair that tests it ('#\6d ain h1' must fail, '#mai\6e h1' must pass) is the only thing that distinguishes a decoder from a splitter that has stopped crashing. If the implementer cannot get both right, stop rather than shipping the one that makes the suite green on '#\6d ain' — a partial fix here reintroduces a false pass that this order was filed to close.

Layer rank in the cascade is easy to get half right, and each half fails in a direction the other half does not. Getting unlayered-beats-layered for normal declarations but forgetting that !important reverses it leaves '@layer base { h1 { font-size: 2.4rem !important } }' a false pass; getting the reversal but not the base leaves '@layer base { .page-title { font-size: 2.4rem } }' a false alarm. Both are pinned, and the clean tree must stay at 0 offenders with the shipped sheet's own @media blocks now flowing through the same reader.

The value-shaped report rule (approach §5) widens what is silent, and the safe way to widen is not to widen. A shorthand must never be silenced — I measured '#main h1 { font: 700 1.4rem system-ui }' leaving the font-size at 22.4px while dropping the line-height to normal — and ':root { all: revert }' must be the only removal-shaped exemption. If the implementer finds a third case they want to exempt, that is a design decision and belongs in this order, not in a code comment.

The at-rule table makes '@media print' and '@media speech' silent, which is a real loss of coverage: a print-only override of the page title would no longer turn the suite red. It is written into AC-14 rather than left implicit, and it is the one place where this order knowingly trades a report for the absence of a false one. If a reviewer disagrees, the alternative is to keep reporting every @media and accept that T-14 flags one disagreement on every future run — that is a judgement call about which failure is worse, and it should be made deliberately.

The at-rule table's @container row rests on an assumption about the sheet, not on a fact about CSS: that no rule declares container, container-type or container-name. The guard checks the sheet for that, so the assumption is verified at run time rather than trusted, but a container created at runtime by script rather than by CSS would make the check wrong in the false-alarm direction. The app has no script-created containers today.

The reachability function is now asked about pseudo-class arguments it was never written for, and ':has()' in particular is answered 'may match' because the chain has no descendants. That is a guaranteed false alarm for any future ':has()' rule touching the h1, and it is the correct direction under the contract. It is named here so the next person meets it as a known cost rather than as a new bug.

The element chain is read from the rendered markup of one route, so the guard reasons about '/' and assumes the other four shells put the h1 in the same place. AC-6 and the 25-shell test pin that, and layout() is the only producer of the h1, so it holds today. If a future page nests the h1 differently, the failure is a missed report rather than a false alarm.

The whole guard is still a test helper that makes a claim about CSS, which is the failure mode the ticket was filed for. What changed is that the claim is now stated over the whole pipeline rather than over the matcher, so the class of defect is smaller — but a change to the reader, the tokenizer or the value comparison is a change to a guard and belongs in its own commit with its own pinned cases, as v2's case list did not.

.sdlc/memory/patterns/ is empty and this run is a second instance of a shape it has no entry for: a partial reader and a non-decoding tokenizer turning an inability to read into a silent pass, in a guard whose own contract already forbade it. The Librarian's write-up is owed, and the entry should be filed under the symptom QA reports — 'the suite is green on a stylesheet the browser renders differently' — since that is what a future agent will grep for. This order does not write it: that path is reserved.

Modelling the cascade completely. @supports conditions, viewport sizes, prefers-* media, container queries, the full :has() and :nth-* grammars and CSS nesting are all out. Each stays on the 'may match, report it, name the condition' side, which is the direction a guard is allowed to be wrong in. This order closes the shapes that produce a SILENT pass, which is the direction it is not allowed to be wrong in.

alternatives_considered.approach: Patch the five sites where QA's repros land: add '@layer' to the walk() recursion test in readStylesheet, add a '::' check to isClassBranch, special-case ':where(' in stripNarrowing, decode '\\' in splitSimple's name regexes, and leave the value comparison as it is.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: This is v2's approach described more carefully, and v2's approach is what produced the two families QA just filed. Four of the five fixes above are local and correct on their own, and each still leaves the defect class behind it. @layer in the recursion test without layer rank in the cascade trades a false pass for a false alarm ('@layer base { .page-title { font-size: 2.4rem } }' starts being reported, and the browser reads 22.4px). A '::' check in isClassBranch is right, but the same predicate still admits '.page-title[data-x]' unless reachability is asked, so the check is a special case where the general question is what is wanted. Special-casing ':where(' leaves ':root:not(html)' and 'h1:not([data-testid])' as the next false alarms, and each one is already in QA's matrix. And leaving the value comparison alone keeps 'h1[data-testid] { font-size: 1.4rem }' reported with a self-refuting message. The pattern across all five is that a local fix states a case rather than a rule, which is exactly how v2's own case list came to be wrong twice in directions only rendering revealed.

alternatives_considered.approach: Descend into every at-rule, treat all of them like @media, and let the reachability function decide everything inside them.

A rule table with a reason per row is more code and it is the version that agrees with the browser in both directions.

assumptions: The guard's subject is the page as served in a browser on screen, which is the environment AC-1 and AC-6 are verified in and the environment the previous order's browser numbers were all taken in. '@media print' and '@media speech' are treated as proofs of non-match on that basis. If the project's intent is that the guard models every medium, that is a different contract and this one is wrong for print — it is stated in AC-14 so the decision is visible rather than buried.

The document root's font-size is the user-agent default (16px) unless a rule in src/web/styles.css moves it, because that is what makes the page title's 1.4rem read 22.4px. ':root { all: revert }' is silent on the strength of that: revert can only move the root back toward it. 2 — One quote- and bracket-aware splitter. Replace both uses of /\s*>\s*|\s+/ with a scanner that walks the branch character by character, tracking a bracket/paren depth and a quote state, and only breaks on whitespace, '>', '+' or '~' at depth 0 outside quotes. Both the matcher and the specificity function must use this one splitter, or they can drift on the same selector. This is what closes BUG-4: 'h1[data-x="a b"]' is one compound, and because the shipped h1 carries no data-x the rule is then provably unable to match it. My prototype of exactly this splitter needed one correction before it was right — 'main > h1' has a space either side of the '>', and a naive scan emits an empty compound between them and then fails to match; the implementer should expect that and handle it, because it is silent rather than loud.

3 — Match a compound against an element, and the branch against the chain. compoundMatches(compound, element) walks the simple selectors with #id, .class, [attr] (with = ~= ^= $= *= |=), type and * forms, returning false on a proof, true on a match, and undecided otherwise. matchCompounds then requires the rightmost compound to match the target element and each compound to its left to match an element to the left of the one it qualifies — a descendant anywhere in the chain, the element immediately before it for '>'. This is what closes BUG-3: '.page-title h1' needs an ancestor carrying .page-title, and the chain is html < body < main#main < h1, so the rule is provably a no-op and the guard stays quiet.

4 — Make the reachability answer one-directional, and delete mayReachPageTitle. branchReaches(branch, chain, target) returns false ONLY on a proof of non-match, and true in every other case, including every case the vocabulary cannot decide. It takes the chain element the rightmost compound must match, so the same primitive answers both questions below.
  - a pseudo-class is undecidable from markup, so strip it and decide on the base. Because :not(), :is(), :has() and pseudo-classes in general only remove or re-target and never add, a base that matches nothing PROVES the original matches nothing; a base that matches leaves the answer true (may match), which reports the rule rather than guessing. So 'h1:hover' and 'h1:not(.x)' are reported and '.checklist li:not(.x)' is skipped, neither throwing.
  - a pseudo-element styles a generated box, never the element itself, so a branch containing '::' is false.
  - '+' and '~' need sibling information the chain does not carry. Decide the rightmost compound first, because that much is provable with no tree ('h1 + p' is false, since the page h1 is not a p); anything that gets past it returns true.
This removes the whitelist that caused BUG-1 and the throw that caused BUG-4. The rule the guard now implements, stated once, because AC-11, the tests and the failure message must not disagree about it. A rule is REPORTED when either ground holds: (a) it may match the page h1 AND outranks the page-title class rule on font-size, line-height or a top margin — higher specificity, or equal and later, and !important outranks specificity asymmetrically; or (b) it may match the ROOT element (chain[0]) and declares font-size or the font shorthand. Keep the three existing literal assertions in the declaration test — the values must stay visible in the test, not only in a table.

The shipped stylesheet is unaffected: its only root-reaching rules are ':root' (custom properties) and '*' (box-sizing), so the clean tree stays CLEAN.
